newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rangers rescue Japanese climber from McKinley.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rangers rescue Japanese climber from McKinley.

text.p: Park rangers evacuated an ailing Japanese climber from Mount McKinley Wednesday after the man was stricken by altitude sickness, hypothermia and stomach pains, the U.S. National Park Service said.
Rescued at 18,200-foot (5,500-metre) was Hiroyuki Hoshino, 56, of Machida, Japan, the Park Service said.

Hoshino was rescued by a mountaineering ranger stationed at the peak's 14,000-foot (4,200-metre) level; he was flown off the mountain by helicopter, then driven by ambulance to a clinic in nearby Palmer, Alaska, the Park Service said.
Hoshino had limited high-altitude climbing experience, the Park Service said. His most pressing ailment was cerebral edema, an altitude-induced accumulation of fluid in the brain, officials said.
Volunteer rescuers also helped Hoshino's two Japanese companions descend to a lower elevation, the Park Service said.

J.D. Swed, chief mountaineering ranger for Denali National Park, said Hoshino was evacuated just as a storm was poised to blast the mountain's upper reaches and make further helicopter flights there impossible.
McKinley, which rises to 20,320 feet (6,194 metres), is North America's tallest peak.
This was the eighth rescue this summer on McKinley. One climber has died on the mountain this season, and one was killed on adjacent Mount Hunter, which rises to 14,573 feet (4,442 metres).

The climbing season runs from April to July. This year 1,078 climbers have registered to attempt the peak, the Park Service said. So far, 228 climbers have reached the mountain's summit, the Park Service said.
